questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a disaster recovery plan, distinct from the HA/DR technologies covered earlier in this course?
options: A document defining which technologies protect which systems, who's responsible, defined objectives, and exact recovery steps
Another name for Always On Availability Groups
A single backup job that runs nightly
A tool built into SQL Server Management Studio
questions.explain: The DR plan is the document that ties technology to objectives, roles, and procedures — not another failover mechanism itself.

questions.q: Why does a DR plan need a system and dependency inventory, per this lesson?
options: A database depends on things like linked servers, jobs, and other databases — recovering it without knowing those dependencies can leave the business down despite a successful restore
It's only needed for documentation compliance, with no practical recovery value
SQL Server requires an inventory file to perform any restore
It replaces the need for RPO/RTO objectives
questions.explain: Databases don't exist in isolation; a complete inventory of dependencies is necessary to recover a working system, not just a restored database.

questions.q: Per this lesson, who should set RPO and RTO targets for each system in the plan?
options: The business, not guessed by IT — and the numbers belong written into the plan next to each system
SQL Server automatically calculates them
They should be identical for every system regardless of importance
They are set once and never documented anywhere
questions.explain: RPO/RTO are business decisions about acceptable data loss and downtime, and the lesson emphasizes writing them into the plan itself.

questions.q: Why does the plan need named roles with backup people, per this lesson?
options: The person usually assigned a role may not be reachable during the actual event, and more people than just the DBA are involved in a real incident
SQL Server requires named roles to perform a restore
Only the DBA team is ever involved in a disaster recovery event
Roles are optional and rarely matter in practice
questions.explain: A real incident involves declaring a disaster, deciding on failover, communicating, and verifying recovery — more roles than just the DBA, with backups in case the primary person is unavailable.

questions.q: Why is 'we have Availability Groups configured' not the same as having a DR plan, per this lesson?
options: AGs are a tool the plan relies on, but without inventory, objectives, roles, communication, and written procedures, there's technology without an actual plan
Availability Groups cannot be part of any DR plan
A DR plan is only about backup and restore, never AGs
Having AGs configured automatically satisfies every DR plan requirement
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that technology (like AGs) is only one piece — the plan needs the other components to actually function as a plan during a disaster.
